analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.25 an hour while giving employers tax credits for hiring workers from targeted groups.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill, which proposed raising the minimum wage to $5.25 in two steps and revamping a federal hiring tax credit; it died in committee in the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour, then to $5.25 after a year. To soften the cost to employers, it would also replace the existing targeted jobs tax credit with a renamed "work opportunity tax credit" that pays employers a 35% credit for hiring people from certain groups: welfare recipients, veterans on public assistance, ex-felons, high-risk young adults in empowerment zones, vocational rehabilitation referrals, and summer youth employees. The bill was referred to two House committees and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage of $4.25 an hour would get a raise to $4.75 about three months after enactment, then to $5.25 one year later. Workers in the targeted groups covered by the hiring credit — families on welfare, veterans receiving public assistance, ex-felons, high-risk young adults in empowerment zones, vocational rehabilitation referrals, and summer youth employees — would become somewhat cheaper to hire because their employers could claim a 35% tax credit on qualified wages. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage for the lowest-paid workers from $4.25 an hour to $4.75 within about three months of enactment, and to $5.25 a year later.

Gives employers a 35% tax credit on qualified wages for hiring people from targeted groups — families receiving welfare assistance, veterans on public assistance or food stamps, ex-felons, high-risk young adults living in empowerment zones, vocational rehabilitation referrals, and summer youth employees — to encourage hiring of people who face barriers to work.

Sets a real employment threshold before the credit can be claimed — the worker must stay at least 180 days (20 days for summer youth) or complete 500 hours (120 for summer youth) — so the credit rewards retention rather than brief hires.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — especially restaurants, retail, and other service businesses — would pay higher wages (and covered employers would face the payroll cost of the increase). Part of that cost would be offset by the work opportunity tax credit, which shifts a share to federal taxpayers in the form of forgiven tax revenue, and employers would bear the paperwork of certification through state employment agencies. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, partly offset by tax credits

drawbacks.text: The wage increase is modest and one-time: it goes to $5.25 and then stops, with no future indexing, so its real value would erode with inflation.

The minimum wage increase raises costs for employers of low-wage labor, and critics of minimum wage increases generally argue this can reduce hiring or hours for the least-experienced workers — the very group the bill's tax credit tries to help.

The work opportunity tax credit adds certification paperwork for employers and state agencies, subsidizes some hires that would have happened anyway, and is only available for a narrow window (workers hired in 1997), limiting its lasting effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a two-step raise to $5.25 an hour for workers at the $4.25 minimum — is real and targeted at the lowest-paid workers, though modest in size and temporary. The cost is higher payroll for low-wage employers, partly cushioned by the hiring credit. The credit itself is a trade-off: it lowers the effective cost of the wage hike for businesses that hire from targeted groups, but it is complicated, time-limited, and partly pays employers for hires they might have made anyway. The bill is a compromise package in which the wage increase is the worker-facing half and the tax credit is the employer-facing half; neither is badly designed, but neither is ambitious.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House committees — eventually at the subcommittee level — and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 1, 1996 with a Republican sponsor and co-sponsor, and was sent to two committees at once: Economic and Educational Opportunities (for the wage provision) and Ways and Means (for the tax credit).

On May 17, 1996 it was referred to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee of the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee — a step that typically signals a bill is being parked rather than advanced.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
Only five members of the House put their names on the bill: the sponsor, one co-sponsor at introduction, and three later cosponsors, all Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — the industries that would have paid the higher wage — are better off because the bill never advanced, since their labor costs stayed at $4.25 an hour for the remainder of the 104th Congress. Low-wage workers gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Amo Houghton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill raising the minimum wage to $4.75 then $5.25 alongside a revised work opportunity tax credit for employers who hire targeted groups.

for.name: Rep. Roberts
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its co-sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee
against.role: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities (now Education and Workforce)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 1, 1996 and sent it to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee; neither the committee nor the subcommittee took further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for provisions in its jurisdiction, including the tax credit, and never reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred, so the party split was never tested; the bill's only recorded support came from a Republican sponsor and three Republican cosponsors, and no chamber voted on it.

industries.note: The bill would raise the wage floor from $4.25 to $5.25 an hour, increasing payroll costs for businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage workers; the bill's hiring tax credit is designed partly to offset that cost.

industries.industry: Employers claiming federal hiring tax credits
industries.note: The bill redesignates the existing targeted jobs credit as the work opportunity credit, sets the credit rate at 35% (down from 40% under the old credit), tightens who counts as a targeted hire, and limits it to workers hired before 1997 or during 1997 — a fresh, time-limited subsidy aimed at the same employer base.
